We further conducted isocaloric substitution analyses by comparing coefficients for unprocessed red and processed meat with those of alternative animal- and plant-based protein sources.   Results: Over a maximum follow-up ranging from 7 to 30 years across cohorts, we documented 62,336 CHD death. After multivariable adjustment for body mass index, demographic, lifestyle, and medical factors, greater intakes of unprocessed red meat and processed meat were associated with a higher risk of fatal CHD, with stronger associations observed among women (p for heterogeneity due to sex <0.001). The HRs comparing extreme intake categories (≥125 vs. <10 g/d) of unprocessed red meat were 1.34 (95% CI: 1.15, 1.55; p for trend=0.003) for women and 1.06 (95% CI: 0.99, 1.17; p for trend=0.009) for men. For processed meat, the corresponding HRs (comparing ≥50 vs. <2 g/d) were 1.39 (95% CI: 1.22, 1.59; p for trend<0.001) for women and 1.13 (95% CI: 1.03, 1.25; p for trend<0.001) for men. Isocaloric replacement of unprocessed red meat or processed meat with nuts and seeds was associated with a lower fatal CHD risk in both sexes. Additionally, in women, the replacement of processed meat with soy products, poultry, seafood, or dairy products, while the replacement of unprocessed red meat with soy products and dairy products was associated with a lower risk.   Conclusions: These findings support global dietary recommendations to limit the intake of unprocessed red meat and processed meat for cardiovascular health, highlighting the benefits of replacing these meats with plant protein sources, particularly among women.

title: TRANSCRIPT THERAPY TO REGENERATE VASCULARIZED BONE
abstract: Non-healing bone fractures represent a chronic medical condition that not only impairs physical function but also significantly impacts the individual's psychosocial and economic well-being. Current treatment options for these patients are often inadequate. Recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP-2) and 7 (BMP-7) are well-studied, FDA-approved growth factors with potent osteogenic properties. However, its clinical use is limited by the high costs of recombinant protein production and the need for large doses to achieve therapeutic effects, which further raises costs and increases the risk of side effects. A promising alternative is to deliver those BMPs via chemically modified mRNA (cmRNA), enabling the patient's own cells to produce the protein in situ. We developed BMP-2 and BMP-7 coding cmRNA complexed with a lipid vector for transfection purposes. The complex was loaded in a collagen scaffold for BMP-2 in a critical-size femur study or into fibrin hydrogels containing calcium phosphate granules for a subcutaneous or critical-size femur defect study using BMP-7. The scaffolds were implanted subcutaneously into nude mice to evaluate their osteogenic potential, vascularization, and innervation across three BMP-7 cmRNA doses (0.036, 0.36, and 3.6 μg). The critical-size defect model was performed in rats. We assessed bone volume through micro-computed tomography scans, transcriptomic analysis, and histological staining for key osteogenic, angiogenic, and neurogenic markers. While all scaffolds demonstrated osteoinductive properties, the highest BMP-7 cmRNA dose produced greater bone volumes at earlier time points, with increased secretion of extracellular matrix components such as osteopontin and collagen type I. A high dose of BMP-2 cmRNA consolidated the femur defect between 4 and 8 weeks. Although vascularization and innervation were observed, no significant differences were noted between the cmRNA BMP used nor in between dosages. These findings suggest a promising future for the application of mRNA-based therapies in orthopedics where a complete bone tissue including supporting structures such as vessels and nerves are induced.

title: Enhancing Yeast Surface Display: UPR, ERAD, and ER Dynamics in Recombinant Protein Production
abstract: Over the past two decades, the display of various recombinant proteins on the surfaces of microorganisms, particularly yeast, has garnered significant research attention. This method is rapid, simple, and cost-effective, combining the biosynthesis and secretion of recombinant proteins with their immobilization on the host cell surface. Proteins synthesized using this technique are transported to the cell surface and incorporated into the cell wall through mild, native processes, avoiding aggressive chemical immobilization methods that often lead to a loss of physiological activity. Surface-displayed proteins are generally more stable and resistant to environmental changes than those in solution. Depending on the promoter used, cells can continuously renew the recombinant protein on their surface or express it only under certain conditions. Additionally, cells carrying surface-displayed enzymes can be easily separated from the reaction mixture and reused multiple times. These enzymes can also catalyze reactions with substrates that cannot enter the cells, facilitating extracellular synthesis and simplifying product purification. However, the main obstacle to the industrial application of this method is often low efficiency, resulting in limited amounts of displayed protein. The efficiency depends on the processes that the protein undergoes on its way to the cell surface, following the same pathway as native secretory proteins: synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), transport to the Golgi, and delivery to the cell surface via transport vesicles. Large amounts of secretory proteins can overload the ER, triggering the unfolded protein response (UPR) and endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD). Despite significant improvements for some proteins, a universal system for all recombinant proteins has yet to be developed. However, the complexity of protein processing and secretion pathways suggests that a single system improving productivity for all recombinant proteins is unlikely. Instead, several optimized systems tailored to specific protein structures may be necessary. This article provides an overview of the processes that recombinant proteins intended for surface display undergo on their way to the cell surface in the endoplasmic reticulum and represent a crucial bottleneck for the successful immobilization of recombinant proteins at the cell surface.

title: Non‐clinical safety of PST‐611, non‐viral vectorized human transferrin, for the treatment of geographic atrophy (GA)
abstract: Aims/Purpose: Complement inhibitors slightly reduce geographic atrophy (GA) lesion growth, yet vision loss prevention remains a challenge. Iron overload worsens retinal diseases like age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), and Transferrin (Tf) supplementation mitigates iron‐induced toxicity, offering a promising therapy for GA (Picard 2015). To avoid repeated intravitreal Tf injections, we developed a non‐viral vectorized delivery platform via electrotransfection of the ciliary muscle, acting as a biofactory for sustained therapeutic protein production in the eye (Bigot 2020). We evaluated the safety and biodistribution of PST‐611, a DNA plasmid coding for human Tf.   Methods: New Zealand White rabbits were divided into two treatment groups (45 μg and 150 μg/eye) and one control group. Part 1 animals received a single administration of PST‐611 or vehicle with a 30‐day follow‐up. Part 2 animals received repeated administration at the same doses with a 6‐month interval and were followed for up to 3 months after the second treatment.   Results: No mortality, abnormal clinical signs, changes in body weight, temperature, or food intake were observed. No significant changes in blood chemistry, hematology, or systemic microscopic findings were found in PST‐611‐treated rabbits. PST‐611 caused no adverse ocular effects. The plasmid primarily localized in the ciliary muscle, with dose‐related levels persisting up to at least 30 days and 3 months after single and repeat doses, respectively. Lower levels were detected in nearby ocular tissues. No systemic exposure was observed. Human Tf was not detected in serum but was present in the vitreous of treated animals at almost all time points.   Conclusions: PST‐611, administered via a minimally invasive proprietary delivery system, demonstrated safety. Following single and repeated administration, PST‐611 localized primarily in the ciliary muscle with ocular exposure to human Tf up to at least 3 months after the repeat dose. The favorable safety profile of PST‐611 supports its further clinical development for GA patients.   References   Picard et al. Free Radic Biol Med (2105) 89: 1105‐21; Bigot et al. Pharmaceuticals (2020) 12(9): 836

title: Plant-Based Antigen Production Strategy for SARS-CoV-2 Nucleoprotein and RBD and Its Application for Detection of Antibody Responses in COVID-19 Patients
abstract: During the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) pandemic, the development of efficient serological tests for monitoring the dynamics of the disease as well as the immune response after illness or vaccination was critical. In this regard, low-cost and fast production of immunogenic antigens is essential for the rapid development of diagnostic serological kits. This study assessed the plant-based production of nucleoprotein (N) of SARS-CoV-2 and chimeric receptor-binding domain (RBD) of SARS-CoV-2 presented by hepatitis E virus capsid (HEV/RBD) and validation of the plant-derived proteins as diagnostic antigens for serological tests. The target proteins were expressed in and purified from Nicotiana benthamiana plants. The resulting yield of chimeric HEV/RBD protein reached 100 mg/kg fresh weight and 30 mg/kg fresh weight for N protein. The purified N protein and HEV/RBD protein were used to develop an indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (iELISA) for the detection of antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 in human sera. To validate the iELISA tests, a panel of 84 sera from patients diagnosed with COVID-19 was used, and the results were compared to those obtained by another commercially available ELISA kit (Dia.Pro D. B., Sesto San Giovanni, Italy). The performance of an HEV/RBD in-house ELISA showed a sensitivity of 89.58% (95% Cl: 75.23–95.37) and a specificity of 94.44% (95% Cl: 76.94–98.2). Double Recognition iELISA based on HEV/RBD and N protein is characterized by a lower sensitivity of 85.42% (95% Cl: 72.24–93.93) and specificity of 94.44% (95% Cl: 81.34–99.32) at cut-off = 0.154, compared with iELISA based on HEV/RBD. Our study confirms that N and fusion HEV/RBD proteins, which are transiently expressed in plants, can be used to detect responses to SARS-CoV-2 in human sera reliably. Our research validates the commercial potential of using plants as an expression system for recombinant protein production and their application as diagnostic reagents for serological detection of infectious diseases, hence lowering the cost of diagnostic kits.

title: Effects of dry matter concentration in grass silage on milk production of dairy cows fed concentrates high or low in metabolizable protein concentration
abstract: Studies have shown that extended wilting of grass before ensiling can improve the metabolizable protein (MP) value of the grass silage, both from increased rumen microbial crude protein (MCP) yield and ruminally undegraded crude protein (RUP). We hypothesised that extending the wilting of grass before ensiling can increase milk and milk protein production in dairy cows. Consequently, increased silage MP can reduce the need for MP in concentrate, estimated as amino acids absorbed in the small intestine (AAT20). To test this, a continuous feeding experiment was conducted, with 48 early- to mid-lactation Norwegian Red dairy cows. Treatments were 2 wilting levels of grass silages: 260 vs. 417 g dry matter (DM) per kg, and 2 qualities of concentrates differing in MP, in a 2 × 2 factorial arrangement (n = 12). The concentrates were low MP (LMP); 104 g AAT20/kg DM, and high MP (HMP); 123 g AAT20/kg DM, supplied at 8.75 kg DM/cow per day. The cows had ad libitum access to the grass silages. The experiment lasted for 11 weeks. The first 2 weeks, where cows received identical diets, were used as the covariate period. Those data together with data collected the last 4 weeks were used for statistical evaluation of treatments. Increasing DM concentration in silage reduced lactic acid, ammonia nitrogen and proportion of methionine in the grass silage, while it increased residual water-soluble carbohydrates, pH, proportion of aspartic acid and rumen degradability of NDF. There was no difference between treatments in daily silage DM intake (13.1 kg), milk yield (30.2 kg) or milk composition. However, feeding HMP increased urea and uric acid in urine, and urea in blood plasma, thereby reduced N efficiency. No major differences were found for rumen pH, or purine derivatives to creatinine index in urine, as indication for MCP. There was significantly more histidine in blood plasma when cows were fed HMP concentrate. In conclusion, increased DM concentration in silage and HMP concentrate did not increase milk production or milk protein yield in this study.

title: #1830 A glomerulus-on-chip to study glomerular cell interactions
abstract: Abstract  Background and Aims The development of effective preventive therapies for glomerulopathy is critically needed. Current pre-clinical research utilizes in vitro 2D cell cultures and in vivo animal models, both of which present significant limitations. Two-dimensional cultures fail to adequately replicate the complex cellular interactions present in physiological environments, while ethical considerations necessitate a reduction in the use of animal models. Although kidney organoid cultures demonstrate enhanced tissue-specific characteristics, they remain insufficient for a comprehensive evaluation of the glomerular filtration barrier (GFB) due to the absence of capillary loop formation. As a complementary approach, the organ-on-chip approach relies on microfluidic to control the organization of the co-culture of differentiated cells [1, 2].   Method We present a glomerulus-on-chip (GoC) fabricated through photolithography, enabling the creation of durable polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) culture chambers. This model incorporates dual-layer PDMS systems designed to mimic glomerular architecture, featuring dimensional parameters that are consistent with physiological conditions with a 100μm vascular space and a 50μm urinary space. The GoC utilizes three immortalized human cell types: podocytes [3] and parietal epithelial cells (PECs) [4] in the lower chamber, and glomerular endothelial cells (GEnC) [5] cells on the upper side of the porous membrane.   Results We propose an innovative opto-microfluidic organ-on-chip, that constitutes a unique integrated system to comprehensively probe complex pathophysiological processes from molecular events to cell/tissue functional behavior in a physiologically relevant environment. Our GoC utilizes immortalized human cell types to reconstitute glomerular organization and facilitate in situ measurements. The model successfully addresses challenges associated with the maturation of the filtration barrier, providing a robust platform for investigating intricate cellular interactions and conducting drug screening.   Conclusion Existing commercial systems fail in accurately mimicking the glomerular organization and lack the requisite versatility for systematic screening of diverse stimuli. Our GoC model, characterized by its innovative design and functional filtration capabilities, represents a pivotal advancement in glomerular research. This approach offers a powerful, animal-free platform for pharmacological evaluation and pre-clinical studies, paving the way for novel analyses and therapeutic strategies in kidney pathology.

title: MICRORNAS AS MECHANOBIOLOGICAL REGULATORS AND BIOMARKERS FOR TENDON REGENERATION
abstract: The remodeling of tendon tissue in response to physical activity is regulated by a complex interplay of anabolic and catabolic signals. Mechanical forces generated during exercise or daily activities influence cellular behaviors, including proliferation, differentiation, and matrix production, which are critical for tendon homeostasis and regeneration. For decades, it has been recognized that physical therapy and exercise are essential for successful rehabilitation after tendon injuries or surgical repairs. However, the underlying mechanisms of tendon healing in the context of mechanobiology remain incompletely understood. Investigating the molecular regulators of these mechanobiological pathways is therefore crucial for advancing our understanding of tendon adaptation to exercise and healing. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), a family of small non-coding RNAs, have emerged as promising candidates for tissue-specific biomarkers of injury, disease, and remodeling processes. These molecules regulate gene expression and protein production across diverse biological pathways. Circulating and exosomal miRNAs have been extensively studied in cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and musculoskeletal adaptation to exercise, particularly in muscle and bone remodeling. However, the role of miRNAs in tendon mechanobiology remains poorly understood, largely due to the low vascularization and metabolic activity of tendons compared to muscles and bones. This limits the pace of tendon adaptation to exercise and complicates the identification of molecular markers for tendon injury or remodeling. However, recent evidence highlights the potential of miRNAs as markers of tendon remodeling and degeneration severity. The downregulation of specific miRNAs, such as miR-29a, miR-29c, miR-210-3p, and miR-140-3p, has been reported in chronic tendinopathy and degenerative tendon conditions, suggesting their implication in such processes. Additionally, we have reported the upregulation of antifibrotic miRNAs, including miR-16-5p and miR-133a-3p, during the early stages of tendon-to-bone enthesis healing, which highlights these miRNAs as potential therapeutic candidates for tendon-to-bone enthesis repair. However, a correlation between tendon-specific miRNA expression and mechanical loading or exercise intensity has yet to be established. Exploring the dynamic interactions between miRNAs and mechanical forces in tendon tissue could provide valuable insights into tendon adaptation, injury and recovery, which could inspire novel therapeutic strategies. This knowledge has the potential to transform tendon rehabilitation and sports medicine, offering new diagnostic and regenerative solutions to improve patient outcomes.

title: LP-63 Making the AOP-Wiki knowledge graph usable across disciplines in toxicological assessment
abstract: The AOP-Wiki is the central repository for Adverse Outcome Pathways (AOPs), capturing structured knowledge about mechanistic toxicological processes. Using and evaluating AOPs requires significant accessibility and interoperability of this knowledge. To improve these, we previously developed a machine-readable, ontology-based representation of the AOP-Wiki. [1] This semantic knowledge graph connects AOP entities, such as Key Events (KEs), stressors, and chemicals, to curated ontologies and external resources. We made this openly accessible through a public web service. As part of the Virtual Human Platform for Safety Assessment (VHP4 Safety) [2] , we are expanding this knowledge graph with new knowledge, and we have been developing additional user-friendly interfaces that support new use cases in chemical safety assessment. Key developments include: • Integrating curated molecular pathway annotations to enable transcriptomics-based enrichment analysis in a reproducible manner • Connecting KEs to quantitative models such as QSAR predictions and biological assay data to support hazard identification at early stages • Enriching KE Component annotations with curated Gene Ontology (GO) terms to improve the granularity of mechanistic descriptions These developments align with the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and contribute to ongoing international efforts to make AOP knowledge more machine-actionable and reusable across regulatory and scientific domains. [3] The utility is demonstrated through the three regulatory case studies of VHP4Safety focused on neurotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and thyroid hormone-mediated neurodevelopmental disruption, highlighting the knowledge graph's role in enabling integrative, reproducible analyses. To serve a wide range of end-users, including researchers, regulators, data scientists, and risk assessors, our services make AOPs accessible via graphical interfaces and programmable APIs. External data sources such as QSAR model predictions and assay databases are integrated through these higher-level tools, enabling combined exploration of mechanistic AOP content and complementary data sources. All outputs follow open science principles and are delivered as open-source tools, along with example workflows and educational materials, boosting scientific impact. This work expands the number of applications of the AOP-Wiki in risk assessment. By using semantic and interoperable methods, it supports new solutions for predictive toxicology and contributes toward transparent, reusable, and animal-free safety assessment.

title: P30-30 SkinMonitor – Microfluidic reporter skin model for the real time monitoring of sensitizing and inflammatory responses
abstract: Animal experiments are the backbone of risk assessment of chemicals and the development of pharmaceutics. However, the translational failure in the development of pharmaceutics, due to the limited trans-ferability of animal results to humans also sheds doubts about the reliability of many animal tests for risk assessment purposes. This and the growing knowledge about cellular pathways drastically increased the demand for animal-free alternatives, and facilitated the development of so-called new approach methods (NAM). State of the art 3D in vitro skin models mimic very well the human skin in terms of differentiation and barrier function and are ideal to further establish NAMs. Currently, OECD guidelines involving in vitro skin models are limited to endpoint analysis. Furthermore, the static culture methods used in these assays do not correspond appropriately to the human physiology. To overcome these limitations, we developed a microfluidic system for extensive real time monitoring of skin responses to test substances, based on our patented reporter skin modelsFor this, the fully differentiated reporter skin models were integrated in a microfluidic platform and cultivated in an incubation chamber attached to an automated microscope. Test substances can be applied topically on the native barrier of the skin model, the stratum corneum, and its reaction is measured in real time with an array of sensors. The cells of the reporter skin model express a reporter enzyme after activation of sensitization signaling pathways that can be detected in the flow-through. Furthermore, optical oxygen sensors were integrated to measure the vitality of the tissue in real time, as well as reporter spheroids that express the green fluorescent protein (GFP) in response to inflammation. For the detection and reporting of inflammatory molecules such as secreted cytokines or danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) released from the reporter skin model, the reporter spheroids were embedded in collagen, placed in small chambers in the medium channel and automatically analyzed. Taking together, the optical and cell-based sensors of the platform enable the continuous, specific and time-resolved analysis of sensitizing, inflammatory or cytotoxic effects of test substances on the skin in one system. With this microfluidic reporter skin system, we provide the base for a more in-depth and specific in vitro analysis that considers different parameters of skin toxicity for the next generation of risk assessment.

title: OS01-10 In vitro/in silicointegrative test battery to detect adverse outcome pathway anchored events of chemical-induced cholestatic liver toxicity
abstract: Cholestatic liver toxicity induced by chemicals is a multisectoral concern and remains a challenge to predict. This challenge arises in part due to a lack of mechanistic understanding of this type of adversity. Additionally, there has been a demand to step away from animal tests towards next generation risk assessment, which utilizes in chemico, in silico and in vitro approaches. To improve the mechanistic understanding of chemical-induced cholestasis, an adverse outcome pathway (AOP) networks has been previously introduced by our team. In this AOP network, the links between molecular initiating events (MIEs), key events (KEs) and the adverse outcome are depicted. The present study set out to build a test battery based on the AOP network for chemical-induced cholestasis by combining both in vitro and in silico approaches. A total of 7 chemicals were selected, including 3 wellknown cholestatic drugs, 2 cholestatic industrial chemicals and 2 non-cholestatic drugs. The in vitro test platform focussed on investigating MIEs and KEs in the AOP network on both the transcriptional and functional level with exposures up to 72 hours. In vitro monolayer cell cultures of human HepaRG cells were used and test concentrations were based on the concentration causing 10% cytotoxicity. The MIE of drug transporter changes was investigated by analysing the expression of drug transporter genes and by using fluorescent substrates. Additionally, the MIE of bile canaliculi dynamics was investigated using time-lapsed phase contrast microscopy. The generic adverse KEs of endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial impairment and oxidative stress were investigated using suitable fluorescent probes. The in silico approaches were comprised of quantitative-structure activity relationship (QSAR), alert-based structural activity relationships (SAR) and molecular docking targeting protein targets associated with MIEs in the AOP networks. The SAR and QSAR modelling classified chemicals based on their inhibitory/substrate effects on proteins. Molecular docking simulated the binding of chemicals to protein structures providing relevant parameters such as binding energy and interaction fraction. Results from the in vitro and in silico parts of the test battery were jointly evaluated and quantified using a weight-of-evidence approach to assess the cholestatic potential of the test chemicals increasing the relevance and application potential. In conclusion, this study provides an animal-free mechanism-based test battery for the prediction of the cholestatic potential of chemicals and the combined evaluation allows for the classification of the chemicals according to the level of concern.

title: P18-89 Bridging Physiological Accuracy and Worldwide Reproducibility: The EpiVaginal™ Model Integrated with Simulated Vaginal Fluid (SVF)
abstract: Regulatory agencies increasingly favor alternative, animal-free methods for safety assessments, creating an urgent need for innovative, physiologically relevant in vitro models. The recent introduction of the EpiVaginal™ model in Europe offers new opportunities for vaginal biocompatibility screening. Our study presents an innovative integration of this human-derived 3D vaginal model with Simulated Vaginal Fluid (SVF), designed to closely replicate native vaginal conditions. We aimed to evaluate not only the irritation potential of common vaginally applied ingredients but also the global reproducibility of the model through inter-laboratory comparisons between the United States and Europe. EpiVaginal™ tissues were simultaneously produced by MatTek in the US and Europe (Slovakia), employing standardized exposure time which reduced tissue viability to 50% (ET-50) quality control assays with 1% Triton X-100 (acceptance criteria: ET-50 between 0.70-1.70 hrs). Inter-lab reproducibility was evaluated by comparing ET-50, %tissue viability, and %barrier integrity between laboratories. Test ingredients included Nonoxynol-9, Benzalkonium Chloride, Benzocaine, Miconazole, Boric Acid, and Acetic Acid at clinically relevant concentrations, exposed to tissues in the presence of SVF for 1, 4 and 18h. Irritation potential was assessed by MTT viability assays, transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and inflammatory cytokine profiles. A total of 40 production lots (20 US, 20 Europe) demonstrated exceptional consistency, with all ET-50 values for 1% Triton X-100 meeting established acceptance criteria, Inter-lab comparisons for ET-50 assays showed high reproducibility. The integration of SVF notably enhanced physiological relevance, providing refined discrimination between irritants (e.g., Nonoxynol-9, ET-50=1.74 hrs) and non-irritants (e.g., Boric Acid, ET-50>18 hrs), strongly aligning with in vivo expectations. Complementary analyses of inflammatory cytokines demonstrated a direct correlation with previously published literature, highlighting significant inflammatory responses particularly for Nonoxynol-9 and ethanol-based vehicles. The lot-to-lot and lab-to-lab reproducibility observed in two geographically distinct locations indicate that the EpiVaginal™ model can serve as a valuable alternative method to screen feminine care products and reduce animal usage. Additionally, this testing approach has been proposed as an in vitro replacement for the rabbit vaginal irritation test for assessing the safety of spermicides and other feminine care products. The inclusion of SVF further enhances this model by closely mimicking the natural vaginal environment, improving the physiological relevance and predictive accuracy of preclinical safety evaluations. The analysis of inflammatory cytokines adds depth to safety profiling, confirming the mechanistic insights provided by this model.

title: LP-40 Launch of the DIM testing project: when animal testing is difficult, impossible and meaningless (DIM) and implications for REACH regulation
abstract: The EU's REACH Regulation Article 25 mandates that animal testing should be used only as a last resort. Adaptations of this standard (i.e. using animal test models) testing regime are described primarily through Annex XI. However, traditional in vivo testing remains common, often due to procedural rigidity and/or lack of understanding or proper application of regulatory framework, rather than scientific necessity. Approximately 5–7 million animals have been used or are in use for new in vivo toxicological and ecotoxicological studies under REACH [1] . The AFSA Collaboration launched a multi-phase project to address persistent misalignments between regulatory expectations and scientific best practices regarding non-animal approaches, with a focus on animal tests that are Difficult, Impossible, or Meaningless (DIM). DIM testing refers to cases where in vivo studies have been performed or requested when they are scientifically unfit, unjustified, technically infeasible, or irrelevant to real-world safety outcomes. Such tests often yield redundant, unreliable or unusable results, particularly for sub-stances with properties that compromise standard protocols, such as volatility, insolubility, or rapid degradation. Moreover, these unnecessary tests might subject animals to distressing and painful procedures without generating meaningful scientific data. The AFSA DIM Testing Project is systematically reviewing registration dossiers and compliance decisions to quantify the prevalence of DIM tests and identify missed opportunities for scientifically sound, non-animal alternatives. The multidisciplinary expert group defined objective DIM criteria for substances (to be) tested and applied them to case studies across sectors, revealing recurring gaps in guidance clarity, methodological relevance, and procedural flexibility. Preliminary findings suggest reliance on animal testing in scenarios where adaptations or modern methods would have been sufficient. Initial evidence suggests that ecotoxicological endpoints seem to be most affected, with high animal use and limited regulatory value. Based on these insights, the project has formulated preliminary recommendations to improve the implementation of the last resort requirement, increase regulatory acceptance of novel methods, and clarify when standard animal tests are inappropriate. As the European Commission prepares the REACH revision, this work highlights a timely opportunity to strengthen enforcement of Article 25, modernise testing frameworks, and uphold REACH's ethical and scientific commitments. A regulatory shift toward relevance-based, exposure-led safety assessment, rooted in robust non-animal methods, is essential for reducing unnecessary testing while maintaining high standards for human and environmental protection. On behalf of the Animal-Free Safety Assessment (AFSA) Collaboration

title: EFFECTIVENESS OF DIFFERENT SODIUM FLUORIDE CONCENTRATIONS AGAINST LACTOBACILLUS CASEI IN THE INHIBITION ZONE: A NOVEL INOCULATION MICROBIOLOGICAL STUDY
abstract: Background: Lactobacillus Casei is a bacterium related to dental caries by producing acidification of the oral environment and leading to teeth demineralization. It appears that these bacteria correlate with another pathogenic microorganism, as evidenced by increased extracellular protein production. Sodium fluoride has been used as a preventive treatment to prevent acidification and reduce the risk of caries disease. At the same time, the optimal sodium fluoride concentration for prevention and treatment remains unclear, which also allows for safety in dental products. The present trial aims to find the best sodium fluoride concentration that is effective in eliminating Lactobacillus Casei. Methods: To evaluate the inhibitory effect of sodium fluoride on Lactobacillus casei, we conducted a preliminary trial using distilled water (0% sodium fluoride) to refine experimental procedures. This trial revealed contamination from airborne dust, prompting adjustments such as working near a Bunsen burner flame to create a sterile environment and manually sterilizing all equipment with ethanol before and after use. Bacterial inoculation involved evenly spreading L. casei from yogurt onto MRS agar plates using sterile cotton swabs. Filter paper discs were prepared by dipping them into sodium fluoride solutions of varying concentrations (0.15%, 0.30%, 0.45%, and 0.60%) and placed on the agar. Plates were incubated at 32.5°C for 72 hours. The radius of the inhibition zone around each disc was measured using a digital caliper, and results were averaged for each concentration. Sodium fluoride solutions were prepared through serial dilutions, starting from 99% sodium fluoride powder mixed with distilled water. Results: The results demonstrated a strong positive correlation (r = 0.942) between the sodium fluoride concentration and the radius of the inhibition zone, as illustrated by the non-linear trend in the processed data. At 0% sodium fluoride, a small inhibition zone (mean 0.58 mm) was observed due to contamination, but with increasing concentrations, the inhibition zone expanded significantly, peaking at 3.30 mm for 0.60% sodium fluoride. Standard deviations were minimal for most concentrations, indicating homogeneity in the data, except for 0% and 0.45%, which showed greater variability. The statistical analysis confirmed the significance of the correlation (p = 0.016), rejecting the null hypothesis and supporting the alternative hypothesis that higher sodium fluoride concentrations inhibit bacterial growth more effectively. Error bars highlighted the precision of the data, with the lowest error observed at 0.30% sodium fluoride (0.11 mm). Conclusion: The most effective concentration of sodium fluoride was 0.60%. This concentration obtained the widest zone of inhibition against Lactobacillus Cassei, followed by 0.45% concentration.

title: P18-91 Exploring PoD-NAMs for DNT Risk Assessment: Bridging In vitro Data and Human Exposure Levels
abstract: Quantitative in vitro to in vivo extrapolation (QIVIVE) is a methodology that links in vitro concentration-effect relationships to in vivo organ exposure, ultimately translating these findings into equivalent human exposure levels. QIVIVE dosimetry assumes that a chemical will behave similarly in an in vitro system as it would in the blood or tissue of a living organism. The accuracy of this assumption depends on appropriately accounting for vitro kinetic factors, such as chemical binding to proteins and lipids, as well as the in vivo absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) processes, which require the use of biokinetic modeling approaches. In silico mass balance models are employed to simulate chemical distribution within the in vitro system, while physiologically based kinetic (PBK) models are used to simulate in vivo kinetics and estimate the exposure dose required to achieve a target tissue or plasma concentration equivalent to the in vitro concentration. By benchmarking the predicted external doses against potential human exposure scenarios, it is possible to estimate potential health risks. With the focus on New Approach Methods (NAMs), the aim of this work is to compare Points of Departure (PoDs) based on in vitro Developmental Neurotoxicity (DNT) data (PoD-NAMs) to traditional PoDs derived from animal DNT studies, specifically for a group of selected pesticides. DNT in vitro concentration-response data were translated into equivalent human dose-response curves, using PBK model-facilitated reverse dosimetry. Various scenarios were explored, focusing on different in vitro starting points and in vivo surrogates for extrapolation such as using medium unbound concentrations as surrogate for fetus plasma concentrations, in order to quantify the differences between the approaches. For simulating the in vitro kinetics, silico biokinetic models specifically designed for DNT assays, and developed in the ONTOX project, were utilized. PBK models of varying complexity were applied, ranging from simple high-throughput models to models more tailored to the specific chemicals. The results suggest that while parameters describing systemic availability (such as oral permeability and clearance) significantly influence QIVIVE, the choice of the different dose metrics also plays a major role. The selection of the dosimetry to be used should also consider the significant uncertainties surrounding the fetal blood-brain barrier (BBB) development, as well as the exposure prior to placental formation. Hence, the appropriate QIVIVE workflow may vary depending on the chemical and gestation exposure window. Ultimately, the PoD-NAMs derived will be compared to European dietary exposure levels to estimate DNT-related risks due to pesticide exposure. This work provides valuable case study examples using a tiered QIVIVE-DNT methodology, thereby facilitating the transition towards Next-Generation Risk Assessment and animal-free DNT risk assessment.

title: P28-04 Towards Animal-Free DIT Testing: Establishing a Human Stem Cell-Based Assay for Early Hematopoiesis
abstract: The mammalian immune system is a highly complex and interactive network of cells that orchestrates both innate and adaptive immune responses. The neonatal immune system is potentially more vulnerable to chemical disruption than its adult counterpart. Consequently, immunotoxic effects occurring during early development may go undetected in studies conducted exclusively in adult animals. Under regulatory frameworks such as EU REACH, the requirement for developmental immunotoxicity (DIT) studies – e.g. inclusion of DIT cohorts in OECD TG 443 – is typically determined based on a weight-of-evidence approach from supporting studies. However, DIT studies are resource-intensive, time-consuming, and involve a large number of animals. Adding further complexity, species-specific differences in immune system development pose significant challenges for extrapolating findings from rodents to humans. In line with the European Green Deal and global efforts to reduce animal testing, this project contributes to the long-term goal of developing a human cell-based in vitro test battery (IVB) for DIT assessment. As a foundational resource to support the design of such human-relevant approaches, we developed the Human Immune System Development map (HIDmap) – a curated, visual representation of prenatal immune development. The HIDmap integrates literature-based knowledge on immune cell types, migratory processes, molecular signaling, and organ-specific niches, providing a structured framework to inform the creation of New Approach Methodologies (NAM)-based DIT assays. As an initial step toward the development of the IVB, we focus on modeling the earliest stage of human hematopoiesis using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and their differentiation into hematopoietic stem cells (iHSCs). Differentiation was performed using a commercially available kit (StemCell Technologies), in the presence or absence of selected potential DIT compounds. On day 12, iHSCs were analyzed by flow cytometry for hematopoietic stem cell markers CD34 and CD43. In parallel, cytotoxicity (Annexin V+/PI+ and PI+ cell populations) and proliferation (Ki-67+) were evaluated. Our results demonstrate the successful and reproducible differentiation of hiPSCs into iHSCs within 12 days. Moreover, we established key assay components needed for regulatory method development, including endpoint-specific negative and positive controls for iHSC differentiation, as well as positive controls for the endpoints of proliferation and cytotoxicity. This study represents a crucial first step toward the development of a human-relevant in vitro DIT IVB, with a specific focus on the critical developmental window of hematopoiesis. In the next phase, the assay will be challenged with a training set of known DIT-positive and -negative compounds. Additionally, an endpoint assessing iHSC migration will be integrated to further expand the assay's applicability and predictive value.

title: S15-01 Building a virtual human for chemical risk assessment from software and data; integrating reproducible research and predictive modelling
abstract: The ever-increasing scientific body of knowledge on health and disease, together with the ongoing development of innovative in vitro and in silico Non-Animal Methods (NAM), offer opportunities for animal-free safety assessment. To fully leverage the promise of NAMs and at the same time ensure safety, intersectoral and -disciplinary collaborations are necessary. This is explored in the Virtual Human Platform for Safety Assessment project (VHP4Safety). VHP4Safety is a Dutch funded research project that runs from 2021 to 2026 and brings together international partners from 32 organisations representing scientists, industry, regulators, policy makers, clinicians and Non-Animal Methods. During the projects’ Designathons and Hackathons, data scientists, toxicologists and social scholars collaborate: (1) to build a data infrastructure to integrate existing and newly developed data and services at the Virtual Human Platform (VHP), (2) to feed the VHP with toxicological knowledge and NAM data and (3) to implement the VHP taking into account stakeholder perspectives [1] . Here, we will demonstrate how principles of reproducible science are applied throughout the development of the VHP. We will address the most crucial technical solutions to build, test and host the VHP platform, using open science community standards. To build the VHP, an interdiciplinary development team with mixed expertise in bioinformatics, cheminformatics, molecular biology, artificial intelligence, toxicology, statistics and cloud development, work together in short sprints to deliver tangible minimal-viable products. The team has recently adopted an Agile way of working and we will share some insights on the benefits of using such an approach above the more classical ‘waterfall’ project stucture. The VHP consists of artifacts being: software, models, documentation, standard operating procedures, workflows and data. In this presentation we will dive into how we are structuring these artifacts to form a coherent and user-friendly platform that can be used to address chemical risk-assessment questions. The VHP design and implementation is revolving around three specific case-studies: thyroid toxicity, kidney toxicity and neuro-toxicity. These case studies guide the direction of the platform development and are aimed at showcasing its capabilities. We will focus on how we are generating a sustainable platform in terms of reuse and the ability to further the develop the VHP after project end. We will showcase specific technologies that are geared towards sharing all the artifacts in the platform in a reproducible and consistent manner. The VHP4Safety project is funded by the Netherlands Research Council (NWO) Netherlands Research Agenda: Research on Routes by Consortia (NWA-ORC 1292.19.272).

title: Multiplex and complementary datasets are vital to dynamic structural biology results
abstract: Decades of global investments in genomic sequencing and structural genomics have produced incredible tools for high-throughput protein production and crystal structure determinations. These generated hundreds of thousands of experimental atomic models from nearly all regions of the biosphere, that have been curated and publicly released by the world-wide PDB. Critically, that rich database fed-into computational methods leveraging artificial intelligence and machine learning developed by Google DeepMind to “solve” the protein folding problem and enabled AlphaFold2 to predict structures for millions of proteins with high levels of confidence. As the old adages go, ‘A picture is worth a thousand words,’ and without doubt, structure and function are intimately linked. Consequently, the structural insights from experiments and predictions are rapidly transforming modern R&D strategies across biology. To date, almost all of the structural experimental data and predictions are static. But life is dynamic, and function requires movement(s). Fortunately, strategies in time-resolved serial crystallography at ambient temperature are rapidly emerging from XFELs and synchrotrons that exploit slurries of many thousands of nano- to micron-sized crystals. In parallel, time-resolved freeze-trapping methods using pure samples in solutions are emerging for cryoEM and microED structural methods. These dynamic structural biology experiments couple together structure and function with tremendous potential for generalization across all of biology. All time-resolved experiments include important metadata about reaction initiation conditions for each dataset and atomic model ultimately deposited to the PDB. Because most of the methods are still under development, the metadata may not be captured adequately, and we can/must do better to fully enhance the PDB. Several large-scale facilities promote capabilities to interrogate the same volume of the sample with complementary probes that include electronic absorption, fluorescence, resonance Raman, and X-ray emission spectroscopy (XES). This data is sometimes collected before, during, and/or after X-ray exposure, and it all helps reduce ambiguity when interpreting electron density maps of reaction intermediates. We have developed sample-efficient delivery and reaction initiation strategies that use room temperature microcrystal slurries and serial crystallography methods for time-resolved studies. In some strategies, we simultaneously collect time-resolved serial crystallography (tr-SSX/tr-SFX) diffraction data in the forward direction, and X-ray emission spectroscopy (tr-XES) data at ∼ 90°, using either XFEL (tr-SFX) or synchrotron (tr-SSX) sources. The resulting atomic and electronic structures are fully correlated and have been applied to many types of samples. We envision a future wherein scientist routinely collect time-resolved data across entire reaction coordinates. These results will inform new predictive, AI-based algorithms that include significant dynamics, and thereby enable engineering biology at scale – that is to create new macromolecules with novel structure, function and/or to catalyse new types of reactions in a green bio-catalysis era.

title: Precision Agriculture Current Progress From a Novel Bibliometric Method
abstract:
ABSTRACT Agriculture plays a crucial role in sustaining the global population, providing food to billions of people. As the world's population continues to grow, the demand for more efficient and sustainable farming practices becomes ever more critical. Precision agriculture has emerged as a transformative solution, integrating advanced technologies like sensors, data analytics, and automation. This approach allows for better resource management, reducing waste and increasing productivity, while also promoting sustainability. This study utilizes the latest bibliometric analysis methods to explore precision agriculture's current state and future prospects. By analyzing over 1000 academic articles, this method provides deeper insights into key trends, patterns, and technological innovations shaping the field. The paper focuses on two major themes: optimizing resources for sustainable farming and the integration of big data and machine learning technologies. These innovations promise to enhance farming practices, making agriculture more efficient, adaptive, and capable of meeting future food security challenges.
Resumen La agricultura desempeña un papel crucial en el sostenimiento de la población mundial, proporcionando alimentos a miles de millones de personas. A medida que la población mundial continúa creciendo, la demanda de prácticas agrícolas más eficientes y sostenibles se vuelve cada vez más crítica. La agricultura de precisión se ha convertido en una solución transformadora que integra tecnologías avanzadas como sensores, análisis de datos y automatización. Este enfoque permite una mejor gestión de los recursos, reduciendo el desperdicio y aumentando la productividad, a la vez que promueve la sostenibilidad. Este estudio utiliza los métodos de análisis bibliométrico más recientes para explorar el estado actual y las perspectivas futuras de la agricultura de precisión. Mediante el análisis de más de 1000 artículos académicos, este método proporciona una visión más profunda de las tendencias, patrones e innovaciones tecnológicas clave que configuran este campo. El documento se centra en dos temas principales: la optimización de los recursos para una agricultura sostenible y la integración de tecnologías de macrodatos y aprendizaje automático. Estas innovaciones prometen mejorar las prácticas agrícolas, haciendo que la agricultura sea más eficiente, adaptable y capaz de afrontar los futuros desafíos de la seguridad alimentaria.
摘要 农业在维持全球人口方面发挥着至关重要的作用, 为数十亿人提供粮食。随着世界人口的持续增长, 对更高效、更可持续的农业实践的需求也日益迫切。精准农业已成为一种变革性的解决方案, 它整合了传感器、数据分析和自动化等先进技术。这种方法能更好地管理资源, 减少浪费, 提高生产力, 同时促进可持续性。本研究利用最新的文献计量分析方法, 探究了精准农业的现状和未来前景。通过分析1000多篇学术论文, 该方法能更深入地洞察一系列塑造该领域的关键趋势、模式和技术创新。本文重点关注两大主题:优化资源以实现可持续农业, 以及大数据与机器学习技术的整合。这些创新有望改进农业实践, 使农业更高效、更具适应性, 并能够应对未来的粮食安全挑战。

title: New Insights into Duckweed as an Alternative Source of Food and Feed: Key Components and Potential Technological Solutions to Increase Their Digestibility and Bioaccessibility
abstract: Sustainability is becoming increasingly important in the world we live in, because of the rapid global population growth and climate change (drought, extreme temperature fluctuations). People in developing countries need more sustainable protein sources instead of the traditional, less sustainable meat, fish, egg, and dairy products. Alternative sources (plant-based, such as grains (wheat, rice sorghum), seeds (chia, hemp), nuts (almond, walnut), pulses (beans, lentil, pea, lupins), and leaves (duckweed), as well as mycoproteins, microalgae, and insects) can compensate for the increased demand for animal protein. In this context, our attention has been specifically focused on duckweed—which is the third most important aquatic plant after the microalgae Chlorella and Spirulina—to explore its potential for use in a variety of areas, particularly in the food industry. Duckweed has special properties: It is one of the fastest-growing plants in the world (in freshwater), multiplying its mass in two days, so it can cover a water surface quickly even in filtered sunlight (doubling its biomass in 96 hours). During this time, it converts a lot of carbon dioxide into oxygen. It is sustainable, environmentally friendly (without any pesticides), and fast growing; can be grown in indoor vertical farms and aquaculture, so it does not require land; is easy to harvest; and has a good specific protein yield. Duckweed belongs to the family Araceae, subfamily Lemnoideae, and has five genera (Lemna, Spirodela, Wolffia, Wolffiella, Landolita) containing a total of approximately 36–38 recognised species. Duckweed is gaining attention in nutrition and food sciences due to its potential as a sustainable source of protein, vitamins, minerals, and other bioactive compounds. However, there are several gaps in research specifically focused on nutrition and the bioaccessibility of its components. While some studies have analysed the variability in the nutritional composition of different duckweed species, there is a need for comprehensive research on the variability in nutrient contents across species, growth conditions, harvesting times, and geographic locations. There has been limited research on the digestibility, bioaccessibility (the proportion of nutrients that are released from the food matrix during digestion), and bioavailability (the proportion that is absorbed and utilised by the body) of nutrients in duckweed. Furthermore, more studies are needed to understand how food processing (milling, fermentation, cooking, etc.), preparation methods, and digestive physiology affect the nutritional value and bioavailability of the essential bioactive components in duckweed and in food matrices supplemented with duckweed. This could help to optimise the use of duckweed in human diets (e.g., hamburgers or pastas supplemented with duckweed) or animal feed. More research is needed on how to effectively incorporate duckweed into diverse cuisines and dietary patterns. Studies focusing on recipe development, consumer acceptance, palatability, and odour are critical. Addressing these gaps could provide valuable insights into the nutritional potential of duckweed and support its promotion as a sustainable food source, thereby contributing to food security and improved nutrition. In summary, this article covers the general knowledge of duckweed, its important nutritional values, factors that may affect their biological value, and risk factors for the human diet, while looking for technological solutions (covering traditional and novel technologies) that can be used to increase the release of the useful, health-promoting components of duckweed and, thus, their bioavailability. This article, identifying gaps in recent research, could serve as a helpful basis for related research in the future. Duckweed species with good properties could be selected by these research studies and then included in the human diet after they have been tested for food safety.

title: #274 Genotype of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in Greek patients
abstract: Abstract  Background and Aims Genetic testing in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) provides critical information about the disease, enhances prognostic evaluation, and plays a vital role in patient management. This study aims to investigate the genetic etiology of ADPKD in a cohort of Greek patients.   Method A total of 135 ADPKD patients (62 females, 73 males; median age at diagnosis: 24 years, IQR: 17–34) were included in this study, with 27 patients diagnosed before the age of 15. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed in 104 patients, revealing more than 10 renal cysts. Children with a positive family history (FH) displayed at least one cyst in echography, while two without FH had multiple renal cysts. All patients underwent genetic testing, including targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) of over 600 clinically relevant genes, Sanger sequencing, and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA).   Results Genetic analysis confirmed a diagnosis in 126 of 135 patients (93.3%). Variants in the PKD1 gene were detected in 90 patients (66.6%), with 66 (75.9%) resulting in truncated protein production. Variants in the PKD2 gene were identified in 20 patients (14.8%). The variant types of PKD1 and PKD2 genes are illustrated in Fig. 1. Genetic variants in genes other than PKD1 and PKD2 were identified in 12 patients (8.9%), including GANAB (3 cases), IFT140 (2 cases), and SEC61B gene (2 cases, a father and son, with high hepatic cyst charge), the later classified as variant of uncertain significance (VUS) according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines. In two other cases involving a father 73 and a daughter 35 years old (who had 3 other family members with chronic renal failure of unknown etiology), two variants were identified in PKHD1 and COL4A3 genes, both classified as VUS. Finally, three cases with multiple kidney cysts showed variants in DNAJB11, SEC63, and SLC3A1 genes, which were classified as frameshift, splicing and missense, respectively. Simultaneous variants in PKD1 and other genes were observed in four patients. In three related patients (a father, son, and grandson with typical polycystic kidneys), variants in PKD1 and PKHD1 were identified, both classified as VUS. In another case (categorized as Mayo Imaging Class 1C), a pathogenic frameshift mutation in PKD1 and a pathogenic missense mutation in COL4A4 were detected. Overall, 42.9% of identified variants were classified as pathogenic, 50% as likely pathogenic, and 7.1% (9 cases) as VUS, according to ACMG guidelines.   Conclusion This study highlights the genetic diversity of ADPKD in Greek patients. The predominance of the variants identified in PKD1 and PKD2 genes, particularly those leading to truncated Polycystin-1 production, underscores their critical role in ADPKD pathogenesis. The identification of variants in other genes such as GANAB, IFT14O etc. reveals the genetic heterogeneity of the disease. The findings also reveal the complexity of genetic counselling, as double mutations and VUS are frequently observed, in patients with typical and atypical phenotypes, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive genetic testing in the diagnosis and management of ADPKD.

title: DNA methylation episignature as a novel diagnostic tool for diamond-blackfan anemia
abstract: Abstract   Background Diamond-Blackfan anemia syndrome (DBAS) is a rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome (IBMFS) characterized by impaired erythropoiesis and significant phenotypic and genetic heterogeneity. Diagnosis can be challenging due to clinical variability and the lack of sensitive and specific biomarkers. Over the past few years, several studies have identified characteristic DNA methylation (DNAm) signatures, or episignatures, associated with various genetic disorders, arising from pathogenic variants impacting epigenetic regulation. In recent years, growing number of episignatures have been utilized as stable and reliable biomarkers for the diagnosis of congenital genetic disorders and for the reclassification of variants of uncertain significance (VUSs), and have been implemented in clinical diagnostic laboratories with significant diagnostic utility in genetically unresolved patients with suspected rare disorders. Purpose and methods In this study, we investigated evidence for a DNA methylation (DNAm) episignature in a cohort of 80 DBAS patients with causative variants in various ribosomal protein genes: DBA1 (RPS19, n=30), DBA4 (RPS17, n=6), DBA5 (RPL35A, n=8), DBA6 (RPL5, n=15), DBA7 (RPL11, n=13), DBA10 (RPS26, n=8). Peripheral blood DNA was extracted using standard techniques. DNAm profiling was performed using the Illumina Infinium Methylation EPIC BeadChip arrays (EPIC v.2) according to the manufacturer's protocol (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). Controls were randomly selected from EpiSign Knowledge Database (EKD), at London Health Sciences Centre. Matching of controls and cases for age, sex, and array type was performed using the MatchIt package (version 4.5.1). Results The comparison of DBAS cases with matched controls from the EKD resulted in the identification of a total of 206 differentially methylated probes (DMPs), which enabled the definition of a specific episignature associated with DBAS. Given the clinical overlap between DBAS and Fanconi Anemia (FA), we tested the DBAS episignature in a cohort of FA patients using both supervised and unsupervised clustering approaches. This analysis clearly distinguished FA cases from DBAS cases, highlighting distinct underlying epigenetic differences despite their similar clinical presentations. Furthermore, we developed a specific DNAm classifier for the clinically similar DBA6 and DBA7 subgroups. Additionally, methylation profiles from revertant cases due to uniparental disomy (RPS19:P47L and RPS17 full gene deletion) were consistent with those of non-revertant DBAS cases, with RPS19:P47L showing identical DNAm patterns to non-revertant RPS19:P47L. Applying the DBA episignature analysis to six molecularly uncharacterized cases, three exhibited the DBA pattern. Subsequent genome sequencing identified causative genetic variants in two (RPL5: c.325-380A>G:p.?; RPL26: c.-6+3_-6+25del:p.?), validating the test robustness. Discussion and conclusions This work supports the use of DNA methylation profiling as a valuable diagnostic biomarker in all patients with clinical suspicion of DBAS and critically aiding in the resolution of VUS and molecularly uncharacterized cases. The presence of DBAS episignature in two revertant cases, despite phenotypic correction, indicates that the episignature is a persistent developmental biomarker associated with the underlying genetic mutation, rather than being solely dictated by the current functional status of ribosomal protein production or the severity of the clinical phenotype. Future collaborative efforts via DBA registries are crucial for validating these findings and identifying episignatures for rarer DBA subtypes.

title: Adventitial fibroblasts direct smooth muscle cell-state transition in pulmonary vascular disease
abstract:
Background: Pulmonary vascular remodeling is a progressive pathological process characterized by functional alterations within pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) and adventitial fibroblasts (PAAFs). Mechanisms driving the transition to a diseased phenotype remain elusive.   Methods: We combined transcriptomic and proteomic profiling with phenotypic characterization of source-matched cells from healthy controls and individuals with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (IPAH). Bidirectional cellular crosstalk was examined using direct and indirect co-culture models, and phenotypic responses were assessed via transcriptome analysis.   Results: PASMC and PAAF undergo distinct phenotypic shifts during pulmonary vascular remodeling, with limited shared features, such as reduced mitochondrial content and hyperpolarization. IPAH-PASMC exhibit increased glycosaminoglycan production and downregulation of contractile machinery, while IPAH-PAAF display a hyperproliferative phenotype. We identified alterations in extracellular matrix components, including laminin and collagen, alongside pentraxin-3 and hepatocyte growth factor, as potential regulators of PASMC phenotypic transitions mediated by PAAF.   Conclusions: While PASMCs and PAAFs retain their core cellular identities, they acquire distinct disease-associated states. These findings provide new insights into the dynamic interplay of pulmonary vascular mesenchymal cells in disease pathogenesis.   Funding: This work was supported by Cardio-Pulmonary Institute EXC 2026 390649896 (GK) and Austrian Science Fund (FWF) grant I 4651-B (SC). 
Idiopathic pulmonary hypertension (IPAH for short) is a chronic disease that can lead to severe breathing difficulties and a higher risk of heart damage or other life-threatening complications. While drugs exist to help manage symptoms, none are currently curative. IPAH mainly affects the pulmonary arteries, which are tasked with carrying the blood from the heart to the lungs to collect oxygen. The disease causes the walls of these vessels to thicken abnormally, obstructing blood flow and requiring the heart to work harder. The outer layers of pulmonary arteries are formed of both fibroblast and smooth muscle cells: the fibroblasts produce proteins that support the structure of the vessel, while the smooth muscle helps control blood flow by contracting and relaxing. Both types of cells are involved in vessel wall thickening in IPAH, but what causes them to switch from a healthy to a diseased state remains unclear. To examine this question, Crnkovic et al. compared the gene activity, protein production and behaviour of smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts obtained from the pulmonary arteries of healthy donors and IPAH patients. The experiments revealed that both types of cells showed similar impairments to their mitochondria, the cellular structures that help provide energy. However, differences also emerged. Diseased smooth muscle tissue produced the proteins that these cells use to contract and relax, ultimately impairing their ability to regulate blood flow to the lungs. Meanwhile, IPAH fibroblasts multiplied abnormally fast, potentially contributing to vessel thickening. Growing smooth muscle and fibroblast cells together in the laboratory allowed Crnkovic et al. to examine how interactions between these cells could help drive the disease. This showed that the fibroblasts released signals which triggered IPAH-characteristic changes in normally healthy smooth muscle cells. As such, the ability of fibroblasts to ‘talk’ to smooth muscle cells could be important in the progression of the condition. Crnkovic et al. hope that these findings will help develop better treatments to stop or reverse the progression of IPAH. However, further research is needed to confirm which biological processes should be targeted, and to ensure that reversing the abnormal changes in lung blood vessels is both safe and effective.

title: A direct experimental test of Ohno’s hypothesis
abstract:
Gene duplication drives evolution by providing raw material for proteins with novel functions. An influential hypothesis by Ohno (1970) posits that gene duplication helps genes tolerate new mutations and thus facilitates the evolution of new phenotypes. Competing hypotheses argue that deleterious mutations will usually inactivate gene duplicates too rapidly for Ohno’s hypothesis to work. We experimentally tested Ohno’s hypothesis by evolving one or exactly two copies of a gene encoding a fluorescent protein in Escherichia coli through several rounds of mutation and selection. We analyzed the genotypic and phenotypic evolutionary dynamics of the evolving populations through high-throughput DNA sequencing, biochemical assays, and engineering of selected variants. In support of Ohno’s hypothesis, populations carrying two gene copies displayed higher mutational robustness than those carrying a single gene copy. Consequently, the double-copy populations experienced relaxed purifying selection, evolved higher phenotypic and genetic diversity, carried more mutations and accumulated combinations of key beneficial mutations earlier. However, their phenotypic evolution was not accelerated, possibly because one gene copy rapidly became inactivated by deleterious mutations. Our work provides an experimental platform to test models of evolution by gene duplication, and it supports alternatives to Ohno’s hypothesis that point to the importance of gene dosage. 
Inside all living things, genes carry instructions to make and maintain the body. Individuals carefully maintain their set of genes, known as the genome, to pass their appearance and other traits on to the next generation. Sometimes a particular gene may be duplicated so that cells end up with an extra copy in their genome. Typically, around 50% of genes are duplicated in genomes and these duplicates may then accumulate changes (or “mutations”) that enable them to adopt new roles in the body. Some mutations may be harmful to the body and lead to the mutated gene being inactivated. In 1970, the researcher Susumu Ohno proposed that when two copies of the same gene are present, they can accumulate more mutations than a single copy would while maintaining function. As a result, duplicated genes may thus evolve new properties and roles in the body more rapidly than single-copy genes. However, it has been difficult to design experiments to test this hypothesis.  A protein known as GFP emits green light when it absorbs certain colors of light, a phenomenon known as fluorescence. To test Ohno’s hypothesis, Mihajlovic et al. developed an experimental system to place one or two copies of the gene that encodes GFP into bacteria known as Escherichia coli . The team then introduced mutations into these genes and simulated evolution by selecting bacteria on their ability to emit green, blue or both lights.  The experiments found that part of Ohno’s hypothesis is correct. Bacteria with two gene copies were more likely to retain their ability to emit green light after mutations than bacteria with one copy. However, gene duplication did not accelerate the evolution of more fluorescent GFPs or of new functions of the protein, such as emitting blue light. Instead, one copy of the gene often became inactivated by harmful mutations. This suggests that there may be other reasons beyond those proposed by Ohno to explain why gene duplications are so common in nature – for instance, by enhancing protein production. The experimental system developed in this work serves as a platform for further investigations into Ohno’s hypothesis, which may help us better understand the origins of genetic diversity in bacteria and other forms of life.

title: The surrounding landscape affects ecosystem multifunctionality in oilseed rape fields
abstract:
Abstract    Designing agricultural landscapes that provide multiple ecosystem functions is an important goal for system resilience and future food security. Landscape composition and configuration play an important role in the conservation and distribution of organisms that provide ecosystem functions. They can therefore be fundamental factors for designing agroecological systems. However, little is known about how the landscape can improve ecosystem multifunctionality in arable cropland.   The aim of this study was to assess the effect of landscape composition on multifunctionality and individual ecosystem functions in oilseed rape fields. Multifunctionality was estimated as the simultaneous expression of five ecosystem functions related to crop production (pollination, natural pest and weed control, organic matter decomposition and litter stabilisation) in 94 oilseed rape fields distributed along gradients of grassland, woody habitats and organic farming cover in the surrounding landscapes.   We investigated the effect of landscape on multifunctionality and ecosystem functions using a GLM framework in which the spatial extent of the effects was estimated with the SILAND package. We found that the amount of oilseed rape improved average multifunctionality in oilseed rape fields, while the surrounding organic farming decreased it. On the contrary, we did not find any landscape effect on the threshold multifunctionality. The function‐by‐function analysis showed a quadratic effect of the surrounding oilseed rape and a positive effect of forest on both pollination and weed seed predation. Surrounding organic farming decreased weed seed predation but increased pollination and aphid predation. Semi‐natural habitats had contrasted effects on the aboveground functions, generally increasing pollination but decreasing weed and aphid predation rates.    Synthesis and applications . Our findings suggest that diverse landscapes are required to ensure the simultaneous delivery of a bundle of ecosystem functions in oilseed rape fields. Altogether, our findings indicate that landscape management should not only promote different semi‐natural elements but also should target limitation of dilution effects. Such trade‐offs among landscape metrics for the provision of a bundle of services can lead to optimal scenarios: in our study site, for instance, an oilseed rape cover lower than 10% within a 600 m radius can improve multifunctionality in oilseed rape fields.    
Résumé    Concevoir des paysages agricoles capables de fournir plusieurs fonctions écosystémiques est essentiel pour renforcer la résilience des systèmes de production et la sécurité alimentaire. La composition et la configuration du paysage influencent l'abondance et la distribution des organismes qui assurent ces fonctions, et constituent un levier majeur pour le développement de systèmes de production basés sur les principes de l'agroécologie. Pourtant, l'effet du paysage sur la multifonctionnalité des parcelles de grandes cultures reste peu documenté.   Cette étude a évalué l'effet de la composition du paysage sur la multifonctionnalité et les fonctions écosystémiques dans des parcelles de colza. La multifonctionnalité a été mesurée comme l'expression simultanée de cinq fonctions liées à la production agricole (pollinisation, prédation des ravageurs et des graines d'adventices, décomposition de la matière organique et stabilisation de la litière) dans 94 parcelles, situées dans des paysages respectant des gradients de prairies, d'habitats boisés et d'agriculture biologique.   L'effet du paysage a été analysé via des modèles linéaires généralisés, avec des estimations des distances d'effet des variables paysagères grâce au package SILAND. La couverture en colza augmentait la multifonctionnalité calculée par la méthode de la moyenne, tandis que l'agriculture biologique aux alentours la réduisait. Aucun effet n'a été détecté sur la multifonctionnalité calculée par la méthode du seuil. L'analyse fonction par fonction a révélé un effet quadratique du colza environnant, et un effet positif des forêts sur la pollinisation et la prédation des graines d'adventices. L'agriculture biologique réduisait la prédation des graines, mais augmentait la pollinisation et la prédation des pucerons. Les habitats semi‐naturels présentaient des effets contrastés, favorisant la pollinisation mais généralement réduisant la prédation.    Synthèse et applications . Nos résultats suggèrent que des paysages diversifiés sont nécessaires pour assurer la fourniture simultanée de plusieurs fonctions écosystémiques en colza. La gestion paysagère devrait non seulement promouvoir des éléments semi‐naturels, mais aussi limiter les effets de dilution. De tels compromis peuvent conduire à des scénarios optimaux: par exemple dans notre site d'étude, une couverture en colza inférieure à 10% dans un rayon de 600 m permettait une amélioration de la multifonctionnalité dans les parcelles de colza.

title: Building Sustainable Urban Futures: The Crucial Role of Urban Food Policy
abstract:
Summary Urban Food Policies are valuable instruments that cities use to address the multidimensional challenges of food security, food safety and sustainability in urban contexts. As urbanisation continues, these policies offer targeted solutions, involving coordinated efforts by city governments, civil society and stakeholders, and promoting local sustainability and resilience. They are implemented in four types, including substantive (e.g. schools’ canteens and food hubs), regulative (e.g. food safety and hygiene standards on street vendors), fiscal (e.g. tax on sugary beverages), and informative interventions (e.g. campaigns promoting sustainable food practices). As cities expand, they face important issues, such as food access disparities, rising malnutrition, environmental degradation and food waste accumulation. Urban Food Policies can go beyond traditional national policies, incorporating targeted interventions that address and account for the specific issues of urban life. The main key objectives are: ensuring food security and safety, preserving biodiversity and reducing pollution in urban and peri‐urban food systems, food waste management, healthy and sustainable diets, safeguarding cultural identity. However, their effectiveness depends on robust multi‐level governance, collaboration and political will, targeting the local objectives in line with Sustainable Development Goals. Urban Food Policies’ contribution can enable cities to address current and future food‐related challenges in a holistic way.
Les politiques alimentaires urbaines sont des instruments intéressants que les villes utilisent pour relever les défis multidimensionnels de la sécurité alimentaire, de la sûreté alimentaire et de la durabilité dans les contextes urbains. À mesure que l'urbanisation se poursuit, ces politiques offrent des solutions ciblées, impliquant des efforts coordonnés des pouvoirs publics municipaux, de la société civile et des parties prenantes, et favorisant la durabilité et la résilience locales. Elles sont mises en œuvre sous quatre formes, à savoir des interventions de fond (par exemple, les cantines scolaires et les centres alimentaires), réglementaires (par exemple, les normes de sécurité alimentaire et d'hygiène pour les vendeurs ambulants), fiscales (par exemple, les taxes sur les boissons sucrées) et informatives (par exemple, les campagnes de promotion de pratiques alimentaires durables). À mesure que les villes s'étendent, elles sont confrontées à des problèmes importants, tels que les disparités d'accès à la nourriture, la malnutrition croissante, la dégradation de l'environnement et l'accumulation du gaspillage alimentaire. Les politiques alimentaires urbaines peuvent aller au‐delà des politiques nationales traditionnelles, en intégrant des interventions ciblées qui abordent et prennent en compte les problèmes spécifiques de la vie urbaine. Les principaux objectifs clés sont d'assurer la sécurité et la sûreté alimentaires, de préserver la biodiversité et réduire la pollution dans les systèmes alimentaires urbains et périurbains, de gérer le gaspillage alimentaire, de proposer des régimes alimentaires sains et durables et de sauvegarder l'identité culturelle. Toutefois, l'efficacité de ces politiques dépend d'une gouvernance multi‐niveaux solide, de la collaboration et de la volonté politique, visant des objectifs locaux conformes aux objectifs de développement durable. La contribution des politiques alimentaires urbaines peut permettre aux villes de relever les défis actuels et futurs liés à l'alimentation de manière holistique.
Städtische Ernährungspolitik ist ein wertvolles Instrument, mit dem die Städte die multidimensionalen Herausforderungen der Ernährungssicherheit, der Lebensmittelsicherheit und der Nachhaltigkeit in städtischen Kontexten angehen können.
